w: 1 Never monotherapy: antibiotics alone are not indicated; when they are A professor's hint · 6 questions in the bank Know this Antibiotics are always an adjunct to surgical and non-surgical therapy, given after SRP. Indications: acute infection with systemic signs, aggressive and refractory periodontitis. When to consider antibiotics: an acute periodontal infection with systemic manifestations (fever, malaise, lymphadenopathy: a localized infection starting to spread); aggressive periodontitis, which hits young patients with severe attachment and bone loss in a short time and has to be treated aggressively; and refractory periodontitis, where a patient who has done everything asked (good home care, thorough SRP, surgery, 3-month maintenance) still loses attachment. And always as an adjunct to surgical and non-surgical therapy: "the use of systemic or locally delivered antibiotics is not to be used as a monotherapy in the treatment of periodontal disease." That was his main take-home message. 2 Biofilms: only mechanical debridement removes them; barrier, β-lactamase, slow growth A professor's hint · 4 questions in the bank Know this The dirty-pot analogy: rinses and water piks don't remove biofilm; mechanical debridement does. Biofilms resist antibiotics by a physical barrier, β-lactamase and a slower growth rate. Biofilms are insoluble and stuck to the root: rinses and water piks leave them. Antibiotics come only at the completion of Phase I, after debridement. The putative pathogens live in a biofilm, an aggregation of multiple microorganisms: if one microbial colony is a house, a biofilm is a subdivision in a protective bubble. Biofilms are a trait of supragingival and subgingival plaque. They protect and harbor the resident bacteria, let colonies survive harsh environments, and are insoluble, which makes them hard to remove: rinsing, water irrigation and mouthwashes leave them in place, like a dirty pot left soaking overnight that still has to be scrubbed. That is mechanical debridement: the patient's toothbrush and floss, and our curettes and ultrasonics. Some biofilm organisms survive antibiotic concentrations 500-1000 times greater than systemic delivery can reach. In class he called this the point to "star" and "know for life": the only way to get rid of a biofilm is mechanical debridement. A mouthrinse can supplement it, never replace it. Biofilms make bacteria resistant to antibiotics in three ways: (1) a physical barrier that makes antibiotic penetration difficult; (2) an increased concentration of beta-lactamase inside, which destroys the beta-lactam ring of our strongest antibiotics ("anytime you see -ase on the end of a word, that's what it destroys"); and (3) a slower growth rate of the resident bacteria, which makes them less susceptible to many antibiotics. 3 Doses: his dosing chart and the drug slides A professor's hint · 8 questions in the bank Know this Know his dosing chart: Augmentin 250-500 mg tid × 10 days; amoxicillin 375 + metronidazole 250 mg tid × 7 days; clindamycin 150-300 mg qid × 10 days; doxycycline 100 mg bid day 1, then 100 mg a day, × 10-14 days; metronidazole 250 mg tid-qid × 10 days; minocycline 200 mg bid day 1, then 100 mg bid, × 10-14 days; tetracycline 250 mg qid × 14-21 days. Metronidazole regimens: not under 16. And the drug slides' doses. Amoxicillin plus metronidazole: 375 mg amoxicillin tid plus 250 mg metronidazole tid, for 7 days. The two regimens with metronidazole are not recommended for children under 16, and the tetracyclines are dosed for children only over age 8. A few doses differ from the drug-by-drug slides, so know both: the clindamycin slide gives 150-300 mg tid for 7 days, the doxycycline slide 100 mg once a day, and Augmentin is usually written as 500 or 875 mg. 4 The host response does the damage: bacteria the key, the host the engine A professor's hint · 5 questions in the bank The take-home: it always begins with bacteria. Periodontal disease is not an autoimmune disease; the body doesn't destroy itself without a stimulus. His analogy is the car in your garage. The engine (the host response) is what gets you from periodontal health to periodontal disease, but at two in the morning it won't start by itself. It sits there dormant until someone turns the key, and the key is the bacteria. His one example of a cytokine is IL-1, also called osteoclast activating factor. It activates osteoclasts (bone breakdown: a "blast" builds, a "clast" destroys), stimulates collagenase (collagen breakdown: "-ase" breaks down what it's attached to) and activates PGE2. All of this releases MMPs (matrix metalloproteinases) and more PGE2, and connective tissue and bone are lost: "kind of sounds a lot like periodontal disease." Bacteria can make enzymes that break down periodontal structures directly, but the progression and severity of attachment loss is primarily mediated by the host's immune cells. The host response is perhaps the single most important determinant of disease severity, progression and even response to therapy: host-derived enzymes (MMPs) and osteoclasts upregulated by cytokines cause most of the destruction. Bacteria are essential for periodontitis but insufficient by themselves to cause it. 5 The cascade: pellicle, complement, neutrophils then macrophages, IL-1 A professor's hint · 4 questions in the bank How the body fights back: the cascade starts with complement, a cluster of serum proteins whose primary function is to control inflammation. Complement can lyse bacterial cell membranes directly, but its main job is as a chemoattractant for phagocytes (PMNs). It also releases histamine from mast cells, which increases vascular permeability: fluid and cells leak into the tissue, and that is the edema of inflammation. Neutrophils (PMNs) are the first responders, like the paramedics at a wreck: they arrive within about 24-48 hours of a bacterial insult to remove foreign agents. If they can't keep up, macrophages arrive later. Both are good cells ("if you didn't have them, you'd be dead"), but both release cytokines, intercellular signals that regulate cellular activity, including immune function. 6 Bactericidal vs bacteriostatic; never combine one of each A professor's hint · 5 questions in the bank Know this Bactericidal drugs only kill dividing bacteria; a bacteriostatic drug stops division. Amoxicillin + metronidazole works because both are bactericidal. Bacteriostatic agents inhibit the growth and reproduction of bacteria without killing them, so the body can finish the job. Bactericidal agents kill bacteria directly, but only bacteria that are actively dividing, a narrow window. That is why a biofilm's slower growth hurts our strongest antibiotics. It is also why, when two antibiotics are given at the same time, they must be both bactericidal or both bacteriostatic, never one of each: the bacteriostatic drug slows growth and shuts the bactericidal drug's only window. Antibiotics are classified by molecular structure and mechanism: they interrupt the synthesis of structural components or alter metabolic functions unique to microbial cells. 7 Allergy, cephalosporin cross-reactivity and clindamycin A professor's hint · 6 questions in the bank Know this Upset stomach = side effect. Hives or difficulty breathing = true (anaphylactic) allergy: nothing from that class. 10-15% of adults report a penicillin allergy. Penicillin-allergic and unsure about cephalosporins: don't give one. Cephalosporin-allergic: move on to another class. Clindamycin is usually next (not with colitis). Hypersensitivity is the most common side effect; about 10-15% of adults are reported to have an allergic response to penicillin. Before handing over any prescription, get verbal confirmation that the patient isn't allergic to it. When a patient reports an allergy, ask what reaction they have. An upset stomach is a side effect, not an allergy. Hives or difficulty breathing (the throat closing) point to a true, potentially fatal anaphylactic reaction: then don't give that drug or anything in its class. Cephalosporins: beta-lactam compounds similar in structure and action to the penicillins; bactericidal by inhibiting cell wall synthesis. Grouped in generations (1st to 4th on the slide; a 5th exists) by spectrum and order of development: later generations move from mostly gram-positive toward gram-negative coverage and more resistance to beta-lactamase, so perio favors the later ones. Some evidence of increased bone penetration; may be given with food. About 10% cross-reactivity in patients allergic to penicillin: don't give one to a patient allergic to penicillin who is unsure about cephalosporins. As taught, a patient allergic to cephalosporins has a 100% chance of penicillin allergy, so move on to another class. Cephalosporins can also interfere with oral contraceptives and increase bleeding time with warfarin. 8 Interactions: warfarin, oral contraceptives, digoxin, alcohol A professor's hint · 5 questions in the bank Know this The two things to tell every metronidazole patient: orange-red urine, and a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol. His Van Gogh story (Starry Night halos = digoxin toxicity) is there to make one interaction stick: macrolides can raise digoxin levels. Macrolide interactions: they can raise plasma levels of, and potentiate, many drugs, including digoxin (risking digoxin toxicity), Dilantin, oral anticoagulants (warfarin), cyclosporine, midazolam, corticosteroids and theophylline. Digoxin, a positive inotrope for heart failure, has a narrow therapeutic range. His story: Van Gogh, given digoxin in an asylum, painted The Starry Night's halos around bright lights, a symptom of digoxin toxicity. Cautions: it increases the anticoagulant effect of warfarin (check with the physician); it may decrease the renal excretion of lithium; it is teratogenic, so avoid it in pregnancy. Tell every patient two things: their urine may turn orange-red, and alcohol causes a disulfiram-like reaction with an extreme headache, like Antabuse. No alcohol. 9 Local delivery: the stable maintenance site; PerioChip, Atridox, Arestin A professor's hint · 6 questions in the bank Know this Local delivery's real indication: one site breaking down in a stable maintenance patient, after debriding it. Not a dozen sites (they need surgery) and not aggressive periodontitis. Indications: localized sites that don't respond to Phase I (the textbook answer, "not a great indication"; generalized residual pockets need surgery, not a dozen expensive cartridges) and, the real indication, localized sites in an otherwise stable maintenance patient: one site that was 3 mm for years is now 5 mm and bleeding, a last attempt before surgery. Anesthetize, debride with the ultrasonic and hand instruments, then place the agent, and re-evaluate in 4-6 weeks. Not a replacement for conventional therapy, and not for aggressive periodontitis. PerioChip: 2.5 mg chlorhexidine in a gelatin matrix, 4 x 5 x 0.35 mm ("you don't need to know these dimensions"). Self-retentive on contact with moisture, inserted into the pocket at the end of SRP, biodegradable (no removal appointment). Release peaks about 2 hours after placement, then decreases over about 9 days. 10 Periostat: sub-antimicrobial doxycycline, collagenase, small added gains Review guide · 8 questions in the bank Know this Periostat (sub-antimicrobial doxycycline): 20 mg bid vs the antibiotic's 100 mg once a day. No antimicrobial activity, so no resistance and long-term use; inhibits collagenase from PMNs; the first FDA-approved systemic host modulator, an adjunct to SRP. Periostat is the first FDA-approved systemic (by mouth) drug for host modulation, used as an adjunct to scaling and root planing: the same rules apply, and the biofilm still has to be disrupted mechanically. It is a low, sub-antimicrobial dose of doxycycline (SDD). Doxycycline as an antibiotic is 100 mg once a day; Periostat is 20 mg twice a day (bid), a fifth of the dose. At that dose it has no antimicrobial activity (the bacteria take one look at it and leave it alone), so resistance is not evident and it can be given long-term. Its mechanism is to inhibit collagenase, particularly the collagenase made by the host's own cells such as PMNs, where most of the destruction happens. Take it 1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal and avoid calcium-containing products. It is contraindicated with hypersensitivity to doxycycline or other tetracyclines, in pregnant or lactating women, and in children under 12. Does it work? Many studies say yes. His example is Caton et al., 2000, a randomized, multicenter, double-blind trial. Both groups had periodontitis and got the same SRP; one then took a placebo, the other Periostat 20 mg bid, for nine months, with re-evaluations at 3, 6 and 9 months. The Periostat group had statistically significant extra pocket reduction at every visit (4-6 mm pockets: 0.95 mm with Periostat vs 0.69 mm with placebo at 9 months; 7 mm or deeper: 1.68 vs 1.2 mm) and the same pattern in attachment gain (1.03 vs 0.86 mm; 1.35 vs 1.17 mm). He said not to learn this study's numbers, just what it shows: statistically significant, but is it clinically significant? These are fractions of a millimeter. It helps where we need all the help we can get, in refractory and aggressive periodontitis. Efficacy beyond 9 months and safety beyond 12 months haven't been established, and the net changes were limited. The AAP: adjunctive therapies (systemic antibiotics, local antibiotics, Periostat) are not a substitute for mechanical debridement, meticulous home care and the other therapies that reduce the bacterial load. 11 NSAIDs, bisphosphonates and BRONJ; why to step lightly Review guide · 9 questions in the bank NSAIDs such as aspirin and ibuprofen inhibit the formation of prostaglandins, including PGE2, which neutrophils, macrophages, fibroblasts and gingival epithelial cells make in response to bacteria. PGE2 upregulates osteoclasts and bone resorption, so blocking it is a "pretty good first step." Given daily for up to 3 years, NSAIDs slowed alveolar bone destruction, but daily dosing is necessary: one dose, or a week or two, does nothing. That is the problem, because prolonged NSAID use causes GI problems (a bad gastric ulcer can do serious damage), hemorrhage from decreased platelet aggregation, and renal or hepatic impairment. "We can't just blindly start prescribing NSAIDs" to every periodontal patient, so long-term NSAID use for host modulation hasn't developed. Bisphosphonates are not new drugs. They are bone-seeking agents that inhibit bone resorption by inhibiting osteoclasts, may have anticollagenase effects too, and some studies show changes in white blood cell counts. At first glance, "we just found the magic bullet." The catch is bisphosphonate-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (BRONJ): bone necrosis after an invasive dental procedure (a simple extraction or periodontal surgery counts), with some reports of it happening spontaneously. These drugs are common, given mostly to older women for osteoporosis, by mouth or in high-dose IV forms, and most complications are with the high-dose IV forms. 12 Drug by drug: mechanism, ANUG, C. diff, tetracycline cautions, food Core of the slides · 11 questions in the bank Adverse effects: GI upset is the most common (nausea, vomiting, sore mouth, diarrhea, abdominal distention), and a patient who feels that bad stops taking it. Prolonged clotting time (less vitamin K from gut flora). It is deposited in bone and teeth during calcification: intrinsic stain and enamel hypoplasia (pitting, cusp deformities, more caries), so avoid it in pregnancy and in children under 8. Photosensitivity: tell patients to avoid direct sun. Absorption is inhibited by divalent and trivalent cations (calcium, magnesium, iron, aluminum): no milk or dairy, iron vitamins, mineral supplements or antacids, and take it 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals. Effective only against obligate anaerobes, particularly spirochetes. It reacts with bacterial DNA, inhibiting DNA replication, and is almost always bactericidal. Useful in aggressive periodontitis and ANUG (acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis). Often combined with amoxicillin to widen the spectrum, with highly effective results: both are bactericidal, so they can be given together. 250 mg tid. Food delays but doesn't reduce absorption; bacterial resistance is low. 13 Augmentin, erythromycin, macrolides, pregnancy Core of the slides · 6 questions in the bank Erythromycin, azithromycin and clarithromycin bind the 50S subunit (like clindamycin), inhibit protein synthesis in gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, and are bacteriostatic and generally narrow spectrum. Azithromycin and clarithromycin are more active against anaerobes than erythromycin. Clarithromycin (Biaxin): well absorbed with or without food. It has caused fetal abnormalities in animals and is pregnancy category C: avoid it in pregnant women. 250-500 mg po q12h (bid). ("If there's ever an award for the best smelling antibiotic, this wins": vanilla.) Also flagged in class Bacteria (plaque) are the primary etiologic factor. Smoking and diabetes compound it but can't cause it alone. Antibiotics (via vitamin K-producing gut flora) and metronidazole raise warfarin's effect. You can prescribe; tell the physician and let them decide. Erythromycin: high resistance and near-universal GI upset. Azithromycin and clarithromycin cover anaerobes better. Said again in the Nov 5 class: bacteria (plaque) are the primary etiologic factor. And "definitely know this one": antibiotics alone are not indicated. Gram-negative bacteria are required but not sufficient: the host response to them does most of the damage. Bacteria are the key; the host response is the engine. Periodontal disease is not an autoimmune disease. Deeper pockets, more bacteria, a bigger response, more breakdown: a vicious cycle. Pellicle within minutes; gram-positive cocci first, then the orange and red complexes. Complement calls in PMNs and releases histamine (edema). Neutrophils first (24-48 h), macrophages later. IL-1 (osteoclast activating factor): osteoclasts, collagenase, PGE2, MMPs. Why host modulation goes slowly: turn the host response down too far and an innocent infection could turn lethal. BRONJ: scraping the necrotic bone is trauma, the very cause, so lesions grow. Bisphosphonates stay in the system for years; most complications are with high-dose IV. No bisphosphonate is approved for periodontal disease. You can skip PerioChip's dimensions aren't worth memorizing; know its content (2.5 mg chlorhexidine in gelatin), that it's self-retentive and biodegradable, and the 2-hour peak. Caton 2000: SRP + Periostat beat SRP + placebo at 3, 6 and 9 months, statistically significant but by fractions of a millimeter. Know the point (is it clinically significant?), not the numbers.
